title: 如何减少 LLM 的幻觉
author: Matthew Duffin
content:
Ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

In this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

What Is an LLM Hallucination?

An LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:

  • Making things up. The model fills a gap in what it knows with something plausible. Ask about a product it's never seen, and it may describe one anyway.
  • Getting the facts wrong. The model has the right information in front of it and still misreads it, does the maths wrong, or applies the wrong rule.

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

Why LLMs Hallucinate

A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process says "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

A few things make it worse in your app:

  • Missing information. If the answer isn't in the prompt or the training data, the most likely-sounding text is still a confident answer.
  • Prompts that push. "Be specific" and "always give the customer an answer" reward a guess over "I don't know".
  • Jobs that aren't writing. Date maths, looking up a record, and applying a rule with exceptions are things code gets right every time and models get right most of the time.
  • Long, mixed context. Paste a whole catalogue in and the model has more to mix up, like a colour from one product turning up on another.

Newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

The Costs of LLM Hallucinations

A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:

  • Liability. In 2024, a Canadian tribunal held Air Canada responsible for a refund policy its website chatbot made up, and ordered the airline to pay the difference. Air Canada argued the chatbot was responsible for its own words. The tribunal didn't agree.
  • Professional sanctions. In 2023, two New York lawyers and their firm were fined $5,000 after filing a brief that cited court cases ChatGPT had invented.
  • Privacy. A hallucination about a person is false information about a real person, and it gets stored, shared, and acted on like the truth. The more sensitive the record, the worse it is. AI scribes for GPs, for example, write the consult notes a doctor signs and bills from, so one invented symptom can end up in a patient's medical record and on a Medicare claim.
  • Security. Coding assistants sometimes suggest packages that don't exist. Anyone can publish a package under one of those names, so a hallucinated import can install whatever an attacker put there.

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

What We're Building

Northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:

// store.ts: everything the store knows. In a real app this comes from your database.
export const TODAY = '2026-11-09';

export const products = {
  'ridgeline-40': {
    name: 'Ridgeline 40L Pack',
    price: 189,
    colours: ['Black', 'Slate Blue'],
    details: '40 litres, 55 x 35 x 23 cm, 1.4 kg. Water-resistant 420D nylon, not waterproof. The Ridgeline Rain Cover is sold separately.',
  },
  'ridgeline-28': {
    name: 'Ridgeline 28L Daypack',
    price: 129,
    colours: ['Black', 'Olive Green'],
    details: '28 litres, 48 x 30 x 20 cm, 0.9 kg. Water-resistant 420D nylon, not waterproof.',
  },
  'ridgeline-rain-cover': {
    name: 'Ridgeline Rain Cover',
    price: 24,
    colours: ['Orange'],
    details: 'Waterproof cover that fits the Ridgeline 28L and 40L packs.',
  },
  'summit-2': {
    name: 'Summit 2 Tent',
    price: 349,
    colours: ['Sand'],
    details: 'Two-person tent, 2.1 kg, aluminium poles.',
  },
};

export type ProductId = keyof typeof products;

export type Order = {
  product: ProductId;
  paid: number;
  onSale: boolean;
  member: boolean; // Trail Club members get a longer return window
  status: 'packing' | 'shipped' | 'delivered';
  shipped?: string;
  delivered?: string;
  carrier?: string;
  tracking?: string;
  eta?: string;
};

export const orders: Record<string, Order> = {
  'NW-48213': { product: 'ridgeline-40', paid: 151.2, onSale: true, member: true, status: 'delivered', shipped: '2026-10-03', delivered: '2026-10-06' },
  'NW-48577': { product: 'summit-2', paid: 349, onSale: false, member: false, status: 'shipped', shipped: '2026-11-05', carrier: 'UPS', tracking: '1Z84F2W90352217744', eta: '2026-11-12' },
};

export const policy = {
  returns: 'Unused items can be returned within 30 days of delivery for a full refund. Trail Club members get 60 days. Items bought on sale are returned for store credit, not a refund.',
  shipping: 'Standard shipping is free on orders over $100 and takes 3 to 6 business days.',
  warranty: 'Packs have a 5-year warranty against manufacturing defects. Tents have a 2-year warranty, including the poles and zips.',
};

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:

// emails.ts: six customer emails, each one a different way to trip a support bot.
export const emails = [
  { id: 'green', text: 'How much is the Ridgeline 40L, and does it come in green?' },
  { id: 'waterproof', text: "Is the Ridgeline 40L waterproof? I'm walking the West Highland Way next month." },
  { id: 'sixty', text: 'Do you have the Ridgeline 60L in stock?' },
  { id: 'return', text: "Can I still return my Ridgeline 40L? It's order NW-48213 and it hasn't been used." },
  { id: 'where', text: 'Where is my order NW-48577?' },
  { id: 'price-match', text: 'Do you price match? I saw the Summit 2 for $299 somewhere else.' },
];

The traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 23 or later, which runs TypeScript files directly (on Node 22, add --experimental-strip-types)
  • An Anthropic API key from the Claude Console, in an environment variable called ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:

npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk zod

Every version calls the model through one small helper:

// claude.ts: one place to call the model.
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';

export const client = new Anthropic(); // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
export const MODEL = 'claude-opus-5-5';

// One message in, one reply out.
export async function ask(system: string, user: string): Promise<string> {
  const res = await client.messages.create({
    model: MODEL,
    max_tokens: 16000,
    system,
    messages: [{ role: 'user', content: user }],
    output_config: { effort: 'low' },
  });
  if (res.stop_reason === 'refusal') throw new Error('The model declined to answer');
  return res.content
    .flatMap((block) => (block.type === 'text' ? [block.text] : []))
    .join('')
    .trim();
}

We're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

Version 1: The Prompt Most Bots Start With

// v1-bare.ts: the prompt plenty of support bots start with.
import { ask } from './claude.ts';

export function answerBare(email: string) {
  return ask(
    'You are the support assistant for Northwind Outdoor, an online outdoor gear store. Answer the customer in a friendly, specific way.',
    email,
  );
}

Opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply said it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:

Thanks for your interest in the Ridgeline 60L! Unfortunately, I can't see live inventory, so I can't confirm whether it's in stock right now.

Here's how you can find out quickly:

- **Check the product page:** Stock status is shown next to the size and color options, and it's updated in real time. If a variant is out of stock, you can usually sign up for a back-in-stock email alert there.
- **Contact our customer service team:** They can check current inventory and tell you whether a restock is coming.

Also, if you're after a particular size (like torso length) or color, check that exact variant, since availability can differ between them.

I'm happy to help with anything else about the Ridgeline 60L, like how to pick the right fit or what to look for in a 60L pack for your trip.

It treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:

  • A product page with a colour selector and back-in-stock email alerts
  • A customer account with an order history and a return option
  • A Returns & Exchanges page, and a team that can "generate a return label"
  • Support "by phone, email, or live chat (all linked at the bottom of our website)"
  • A Sale or Deals page, and a newsletter that might come with a first-order discount
  • Orders that "often take 1–2 business days to process before shipping"

Northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

Fix 1: Give It the Facts

The model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

// v2-grounded.ts: give the model the store's data, and a way out.
import { ask } from './claude.ts';
import { TODAY, orders, policy, products } from './store.ts';

export const STORE_DATA = JSON.stringify({ today: TODAY, products, orders, policy }, null, 2);

export function answerGrounded(email: string) {
  return ask(
    `You are the support assistant for Northwind Outdoor, an online outdoor gear store.
Answer only from the store data below. If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email.

<store_data>
${STORE_DATA}
</store_data>`,
    email,
  );
}

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:

The **Ridgeline 40L Pack** is **$189**, but it **doesn't come in green**. It's available in **Black** and **Slate Blue**.

If green matters most, the smaller **Ridgeline 28L Daypack** ($129) comes in **Olive Green** (and Black).

Either pack ships free, since standard shipping is free on orders over $100.

Right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:

**Yes, you can still return it.** Your Ridgeline 40L Pack (order NW-48213) was delivered on October 6, 2026. As a Trail Club member, you have 60 days from delivery to return unused items, so your return window is open until **December 5, 2026**.

Because this pack was **bought on sale**, the return will be issued as **store credit** for the $151.20 you paid, not a refund to your original payment method.

If you'd like to go ahead, let me know and a team member will follow up by email with the return steps.

Delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

Fix 2: Give It a Way Out

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data says nothing about price matching:

I'm sorry, I don't have any information about a price matching policy. A team member will reply to you by email to answer that.

From our store data, the Summit 2 Tent is currently listed at $349. It's a two-person tent weighing 2.1 kg with aluminium poles, and it comes with a 2-year warranty that covers the poles and zips. Standard shipping is free on orders over $100.

It said it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

Why Go Further?

If version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":

  • The model is still doing the maths. Every time a return email comes in, it counts the days, picks the window, and applies the sale rule in its head. It got that right here, but you can't unit test it, and the next model version may do it differently.
  • Nothing checks the reply. If version 2 does slip, the mistake goes straight to the customer, inside a friendly paragraph.
  • It doesn't scale. Sending the whole store works for four products. With four thousand, you're picking which records to send, and that's one more thing that can go wrong.

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

Fix 3: Make It Pick From a List

Version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:

// read.ts: the model reads the email and picks from lists. It writes nothing for the customer here.
import { z } from 'zod';
import { client, MODEL } from './claude.ts';
import { products } from './store.ts';

const EmailRead = z.strictObject({
  topic: z.enum(['product', 'return', 'order_status', 'shipping', 'warranty', 'other']),
  product: z
    .enum([...Object.keys(products), 'not_sold', 'none'])
    .describe('The product the email is about. not_sold if it names a product that is not in the list, none if it names no product.'),
  product_named: z.string().nullable().describe('The product name exactly as the customer wrote it, or null.'),
  order_number: z.string().nullable().describe('The order number exactly as the customer wrote it, or null.'),
  asks_something_else: z
    .boolean()
    .describe('True if the email also asks for anything besides product details, a return, an order status, shipping, or the warranty, such as price matching, discounts, or stock levels.'),
});

export type EmailRead = z.infer<typeof EmailRead>;

// The same schema as JSON Schema, so the API holds the model to it: every enum is a list it must pick from.
const { $schema, ...schema } = z.toJSONSchema(EmailRead);

const CATALOG = Object.entries(products)
  .map(([id, product]) => `${id}: ${product.name}`)
  .join('\n');

export async function readEmail(email: string): Promise<EmailRead> {
  const res = await client.messages.create({
    model: MODEL,
    max_tokens: 16000,
    system: `You sort customer emails for Northwind Outdoor. These are the only products we sell:\n${CATALOG}`,
    messages: [{ role: 'user', content: email }],
    output_config: { effort: 'low', format: { type: 'json_schema', schema } },
  });
  const text = res.content.find((block) => block.type === 'text');
  if (res.stop_reason !== 'end_turn' || !text) throw new Error(`Couldn't read the email: ${email}`);
  return EmailRead.parse(JSON.parse(text.text)); // Zod checks it again and gives us a typed object
}

Zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

Here's what it read from the 60L email:

{
  "topic": "product",
  "product": "not_sold",
  "product_named": "Ridgeline 60L",
  "order_number": null,
  "asks_something_else": true
}

The model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

If all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Fix 4: Let Code Decide

Second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:

// decide.ts: plain code looks things up, applies the rules, and does the maths.
import type { EmailRead } from './read.ts';
import { TODAY, orders, policy, products, type ProductId } from './store.ts';

export type Decision = { facts: string[]; handoff: boolean };

const DAY = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
const toDate = (iso: string) => new Date(`${iso}T00:00:00Z`);
const show = (date: Date) =>
  date.toLocaleDateString('en-US', { month: 'long', day: 'numeric', year: 'numeric', timeZone: 'UTC' });
const money = (amount: number) => `$${amount.toFixed(2).replace(/\.00$/, '')}`;

export function decide(read: EmailRead): Decision {
  const facts: string[] = [];
  let handoff = false;

  const product = read.product in products ? products[read.product as ProductId] : null;
  if (product) {
    facts.push(`${product.name}: ${money(product.price)}. Colours: ${product.colours.join(', ')}. ${product.details}`);
  }
  if (read.product === 'not_sold') {
    const range = Object.values(products).map((p) => p.name).join(', ');
    facts.push(`We don't sell a product called "${read.product_named}". What we sell: ${range}.`);
  }

  const number = read.order_number?.trim().toUpperCase();
  const order = number ? orders[number] : undefined;
  if (number && !order) facts.push(`There's no order ${number} in our records.`);

  if (read.topic === 'return') {
    if (!order) {
      if (!number) facts.push('We need the order number to check a return.');
    } else if (!order.delivered) {
      facts.push(`Order ${number} hasn't been delivered yet. It can be returned after it arrives.`);
    } else {
      const delivered = toDate(order.delivered);
      const daysAgo = Math.round((toDate(TODAY).getTime() - delivered.getTime()) / DAY);
      const window = order.member ? 60 : 30;
      const lastDay = new Date(delivered.getTime() + window * DAY);
      facts.push(`Order ${number} (${products[order.product].name}) was delivered on ${show(delivered)}, ${daysAgo} days ago.`);
      facts.push(order.member ? 'The customer is a Trail Club member, so they have 60 days to return it.' : 'Returns are accepted within 30 days of delivery.');
      if (daysAgo > window) {
        facts.push(`The return window closed on ${show(lastDay)}, so it can't be returned.`);
      } else if (order.onSale) {
        facts.push(`It can be returned until ${show(lastDay)} if it's unused. It was bought on sale, so the return is for ${money(order.paid)} in store credit, not a refund.`);
      } else {
        facts.push(`It can be returned until ${show(lastDay)} if it's unused, for a refund of ${money(order.paid)}.`);
      }
    }
  }

  if (read.topic === 'order_status') {
    if (!order) {
      if (!number) facts.push('We need the order number to look up an order.');
    } else if (order.status === 'shipped') {
      facts.push(`Order ${number} (${products[order.product].name}) shipped on ${show(toDate(order.shipped!))} with ${order.carrier}, tracking number ${order.tracking}. It's due on ${show(toDate(order.eta!))}.`);
    } else if (order.status === 'delivered') {
      facts.push(`Order ${number} (${products[order.product].name}) was delivered on ${show(toDate(order.delivered!))}.`);
    } else {
      facts.push(`Order ${number} is being packed and hasn't shipped yet.`);
    }
  }

  if (read.topic === 'shipping') facts.push(policy.shipping);
  if (read.topic === 'warranty') facts.push(policy.warranty);

  // Anything the rules don't cover goes to a person, with nothing made up in between.
  if (read.topic === 'other' || read.asks_something_else || facts.length === 0) {
    handoff = true;
    facts.push("Our records don't answer everything in this email. A team member will reply by email within one business day.");
  }

  return { facts, handoff };
}

For the return email, that gives:

- Ridgeline 40L Pack: $189. Colours: Black, Slate Blue. 40 litres, 55 x 35 x 23 cm, 1.4 kg. Water-resistant 420D nylon, not waterproof. The Ridgeline Rain Cover is sold separately.
- Order NW-48213 (Ridgeline 40L Pack) was delivered on October 6, 2026, 34 days ago.
- The customer is a Trail Club member, so they have 60 days to return it.
- It can be returned until December 5, 2026 if it's unused. It was bought on sale, so the return is for $151.20 in store credit, not a refund.

Every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

The last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

Third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Fix 5: Check Every Reply Before It's Sent

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:

// check.ts: every number, order number, and product name in a reply must come from the sources.
const PATTERNS = [
  /\b[A-Z]{2,}-\d+\b/g, // order numbers: NW-48213
  /\b[A-Z][a-z]+ \d{1,3}L?\b(?!\.\d)/g, // product names and dates: Ridgeline 60L, Summit 3, October 6
  /(?<![\w.]|[A-Z]-)\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?(?:st|nd|rd|th)?(?!\w)/g, // numbers and prices: 189, 151.20, 2026, 12th
];

// "1,189.00" and "1189" are the same number, and so are "12th" and "12".
const normalise = (value: string) =>
  /^\d/.test(value) ? String(Number(value.replace(/,|st|nd|rd|th/g, ''))) : value;

const MONTHS = 'January|February|March|April|May|June|July|August|September|October|November|December';

function valuesIn(text: string) {
  const prose = text
    .replace(/^[\s*]*\d+\.\s/gm, '') // list numbers ("1. Check your email") aren't claims
    .replace(new RegExp(`\\b(\\d{1,2}) (${MONTHS})`, 'g'), '$2 $1'); // "5 November" reads as "November 5"
  return PATTERNS.flatMap((pattern) => [...prose.matchAll(pattern)].map(([value]) => normalise(value)));
}

export function findUnsupported(reply: string, sources: string[]): string[] {
  const allowed = new Set(sources.flatMap(valuesIn));
  return [...new Set(valuesIn(reply))].filter((value) => !allowed.has(value));
}

It's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:

// write.ts: the model writes the reply from the facts, and the check runs before anything is sent.
import { findUnsupported } from './check.ts';
import { ask } from './claude.ts';
import type { Decision } from './decide.ts';

const WRITER = `You write email replies for Northwind Outdoor's support team.
Use only the facts you're given. Don't add any price, date, number, product, or policy that isn't in the facts.
If the facts don't answer part of the email, say so plainly instead of guessing.
Write only the body of the email.`;

export async function writeReply(email: string, decision: Decision) {
  const facts = decision.facts.map((fact) => `- ${fact}`).join('\n');
  const prompt = `Customer's email:\n${email}\n\nFacts:\n${facts}`;
  const sources = [email, ...decision.facts];

  const draft = await ask(WRITER, prompt);
  const flagged = findUnsupported(draft, sources);
  if (flagged.length === 0) return { reply: draft, sent: 'draft', draft, flagged };

  // One retry, told exactly which values weren't in the facts.
  const retry = await ask(WRITER, `${prompt}\n\nYour last draft used values that aren't in the facts: ${flagged.join(', ')}. Write it again without them.`);
  if (findUnsupported(retry, sources).length === 0) return { reply: retry, sent: 'retry', draft, flagged };

  // Still wrong: send the facts as they are.
  return { reply: `Thanks for getting in touch. Here's what we can tell you:\n${facts}`, sent: 'fallback', draft, flagged };
}

If a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

It's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

The Results

This script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:

// run.ts: every email through all three versions. Writes each reply to out/ and prints a summary.
import fs from 'node:fs';
import { findUnsupported } from './check.ts';
import { decide } from './decide.ts';
import { emails } from './emails.ts';
import { readEmail } from './read.ts';
import { answerBare } from './v1-bare.ts';
import { STORE_DATA, answerGrounded } from './v2-grounded.ts';
import { writeReply } from './write.ts';

fs.mkdirSync('out', { recursive: true });
const save = (file: string, text: string) => fs.writeFileSync(`out/${file}`, `${text.trim()}\n`);
const summary: string[] = [];

for (const email of emails) {
  const started = performance.now();
  const [bare, grounded, read] = await Promise.all([answerBare(email.text), answerGrounded(email.text), readEmail(email.text)]);
  const decision = decide(read);
  const written = await writeReply(email.text, decision);
  const seconds = ((performance.now() - started) / 1000).toFixed(1);

  save(`${email.id}-v1.txt`, bare);
  save(`${email.id}-v2.txt`, grounded);
  save(`${email.id}-read.json`, JSON.stringify(read, null, 2));
  save(`${email.id}-facts.txt`, decision.facts.map((fact) => `- ${fact}`).join('\n'));
  save(`${email.id}-v3.txt`, written.reply);
  if (written.sent !== 'draft') save(`${email.id}-v3-draft.txt`, written.draft);

  // v1 and v2 are checked against everything the store knows, plus the facts code worked out.
  const sources = [email.text, STORE_DATA, ...decision.facts];
  summary.push(
    [
      `${email.id} (${seconds}s)`,
      `  v1 not in the store's data: ${findUnsupported(bare, sources).join(', ') || '-'}`,
      `  v2 not in the store's data: ${findUnsupported(grounded, sources).join(', ') || '-'}`,
      `  v3 first draft flagged: ${written.flagged.join(', ') || '-'} (sent: ${written.sent})`,
    ].join('\n'),
  );
  console.log(summary.at(-1));
}

save('summary.txt', summary.join('\n'));

The check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:

Email Version 1: bare prompt Version 2: data in the prompt Version 3: code decides
Green pack No answer, sends the customer to a colour selector Right, and points to the 28L in Olive Green Right
Waterproof No answer, general rain advice Right, suggests the $24 rain cover Right, but no price for the rain cover
Ridgeline 60L Treats it as a real product Right, passes it to a person Right, passes it to a person
Return No answer, invents an account page and return label Right Right
Where is my order No answer, invents processing times Right Right
Price match No answer, invents live chat and a Deals page Right, passes it to a person Right, passes it to a person

Version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:

Hi there,

Thanks for reaching out about the Summit 2 Tent.

Our current price for the Summit 2 is $349. It's a two-person tent weighing 2.1 kg, with aluminium poles, and it comes in Sand.

I don't have information about whether we offer price matching. A team member will reply by email within one business day to answer that question.

Thanks for your patience.

Best regards,
Northwind Outdoor Support

What Doesn't Reduce Hallucinations

  • Telling it not to hallucinate. "Don't make things up" in a prompt does little, because the model can't tell which of its answers are made up. A way out (Fix 2) works better than a warning.
  • Turning the temperature down. A lower temperature makes answers more repeatable, not more true. A model that's wrong at temperature 0 is wrong every time. The newest Claude models don't take a temperature setting at all.
  • A bigger model on its own. Stronger models make things up less often, but not never. Opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price in our test, and it still described a returns page that doesn't exist.
  • Asking it to check itself. A second call asking "is this right?" catches some mistakes, but it's the same kind of model with the same blind spots. A check in code (Fix 5) doesn't share them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you stop LLM hallucinations completely?

No model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

Does RAG stop hallucinations?

It cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

Does a lower temperature reduce hallucinations?

Not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

How do I measure hallucinations in my app?

Collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Wrapping Up

Hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:

  1. Give it the facts, so it isn't guessing.
  2. Give it a way out, so "I don't know" is a right answer.
  3. Make it pick from a list wherever it's choosing something.
  4. Let code decide anything you can write a rule for.
  5. Check every reply before anyone sees it.

The model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.
aiSummary: 本文展示了 5 种实用方法，通过基于事实数据生成回答、使用结构化模式约束模型输出，以及添加验证层，减少客服机器人中的 LLM 幻觉。
oneSentenceSummary: 本文展示了 5 种实用方法，通过基于事实数据生成回答、使用结构化模式约束模型输出，以及添加验证层，减少客服机器人中的 LLM 幻觉。
summary: 本文以为户外装备商店搭建客服机器人为例，探讨 LLM 幻觉问题。文章将幻觉定义为流畅但不符合事实的回答，并解释模型产生幻觉的原因，包括训练机制更倾向于奖励猜测，而非承认不确定性。文章介绍了机器人的 3 个版本，从基础的提示词方案开始，逐步实施改进措施：(1) 直接在提示词中提供准确的商店数据；(2) 允许模型回答「我不知道」；(3) 使用结构化输出模式约束回答；(4) 实施验证检查；(5) 分离不同任务，让模型从邮件中提取结构化信息，而不是生成完整回答。每个版本都使用 6 个旨在暴露幻觉风险的棘手客户问题进行测试。最终版本结合检索增强生成、JSON Schema 验证和系统化事实核查，实现了准确回答。

mainPoints.point: 当 LLM 生成自信但不符合事实的回答时，就会出现幻觉。这通常与训练机制有关：模型受到的激励是猜测，而不是承认不确定性。
mainPoints.explanation: 文章解释说，模型接受的训练目标是尽可能给出正确答案，因此与听起来似乎合理的猜测相比，回答「我不知道」并非最优选择。这会导致模型编造产品、政策或日期，让它们看起来煞有介事。

mainPoints.point: 通过检索增强生成，让回答以事实数据为依据，可以显著减少幻觉，因为模型只能依据提供的信息作答。
mainPoints.explanation: 将商店的实际产品目录、订单数据和政策直接放入系统提示词，并要求模型只根据这些数据作答，机器人便能正确处理涉及多项事实的复杂问题，例如取决于会员身份和购买条件的退货期限。

mainPoints.point: 使用 JSON Schema 和 Zod 定义结构化输出模式，可以让模型从非结构化文本中提取结构化信息，同时防止它编造无效值。
mainPoints.explanation: 通过 Zod 定义严格的模式，将产品 ID 等字段限制为有效选项，可以避免模型编造「Ridgeline 60L」这类不存在的产品。这样一来，错误会以不正确的 JSON 值显现，而不是隐藏在段落中的幻觉。

mainPoints.point: 允许模型回答「我不知道」，并让回答以数据为依据，可以帮助模型妥善处理超出范围的问题，而不编造答案。
mainPoints.explanation: 当客户询问数据中未包含的价格匹配政策时，有事实依据的模型会如实说明自己没有相关信息，并将问题转交给人工客服。这表明，明确允许模型拒绝作答可以避免编造信息。

keyQuotes: LLM 幻觉是指流畅、自信却没有事实依据的输出：不存在的产品、没人制定过的政策、偏差了一周的日期，或者引用了一篇从未发表过的论文。
它们之间真正的差别，归根结底在于需要编写多少样板代码、数据片段如何进行类型标注、是否追踪成本，以及整体的服务器占用。
如果数据中没有答案，就说你不知道，并告知客户团队成员会通过电子邮件回复。
模型不可能知道 Northwind 的价格，所以要把价格提供给它。这就是检索增强生成（RAG）的理念：找到相关记录，并将其放入提示词中。
关于某个人的幻觉，就是关于真实人物的虚假信息；这类信息会像真相一样被存储、传播和用来采取行动。
